constraints.evidence: Slide 10 and slide 9 show company gross margin for every option against the 75% floor (Pro 76.3–76.5%, add-on 76.2%, free-in-Core 71.9–74.4%). Appendix A shows the formula, including the $0.6M platform cost and AI cost. A 76% guardrail is adopted. The $1.73M headroom is not stated as a figure, but the margin arithmetic is equivalent.

Slide 4 sizes the target as +4 pts × $57.6M = $2.30M. NRR points are given for each option, and mobile churn is sized at $2.18M, or 3.8 pts. The mobile-delay churn cost is quantified separately on slide 12, but it is not netted against the headline NRR range.

Slide 8 shows AI cost at the median ($17), mean ($32), adopters ($61) and top decile ($130) against the $149 price. Slide 7 bridges add-on ARR to gross profit after AI cost (−$0.77M). Pro AI cost is included at the full allowance (Appendix A).
The $0.6M platform cost is deducted in the slide 7 bridge, in the Pro and add-on gross profit and payback figures (slides 9 and 17), and in every company gross margin figure.
Slide 9 gives a payback on the $1.47M build (add-on 1.7–12 years, Pro 1.2–3.0 years). Slide 12 and Appendix A show 14 × 0.5 × $210k. The executive summary headline quotes ARR, not payback.

Slides 3 and 12 accept the two-quarter mobile delay explicitly. They cost it at $0.27–0.82M, compare it with mobile-first, and set mitigations: Customer Success outreach, a dated roadmap, and the engineers moving to mobile in Q3. Mobile at 27% of churn and 38% of top feature requests is cited. The headline NRR and ARR range is not reduced for this cost.

Slides 3 and 7 replace the 46% survey figure ($8.06M) with the paywall 14% ($2.45M). They explain the 6% response rate and the 9.4 vs 6.2 seat skew, call 14% an upper limit because of volunteer selection, and scale it to 10.7% ($1.87M) and 7% ($1.2M).

The $0.009 price is fixed through December 2027 and used in all headline margins. The 35% fall appears only as an upside (~76.9%) and is not relied on. A 2028 price rise is flagged as cutting margin (slide 13) and a renegotiation is planned. The size of the rise at which margin breaks is not given.

Slide 6 computes 1,560 contested deals, 7 pts, 109 deals and $0.64M as the upper limit. It halves this to $0.32M for Routewise's 20% discount and rebuts the VP Sales $1.93M figure. The case counts at most $0.6M from competition.

alternatives.evidence: The recommended option. Slides 9–11 and Appendix A size Pro at 20–33% migration ($1.75–2.89M), tier margin with a 500-request-per-seat pooled allowance, and company gross margin (76.3–76.5%). Heavy use without an allowance gives 74.1%. Packs are priced for overage.

The $149 add-on is sized on the paywall test ($2.45M, $1.87M central, $0.51M gross profit) and rejected as 'second best' (slides 7, 9). The repriced variant is not evaluated: a lower entry price, or usage charges above an allowance. The only usage-pricing mechanism evaluated is the Pro packs.

Slide 12 compares mobile-first and Copilot-first on permanent ARR (≤$0.56M vs $0.27–0.82M), revenue timing and when 105% NRR is reached. The Q1 test on non-volunteers captures the demand-read benefit. The document concedes it is a close call and says timing decides it.

Free in Core is costed at 71.9–74.4% company gross margin, negative gross profit and NRR ≤0.8 (slides 9, 10; Appendix A) and rejected. A hard-capped free bundle (~1,070 requests per account) is not tested, so 'breaks the floor' holds only uncapped.

sensitivities.evidence: Slides 4, 9 and 13 give the add-on at 7–14% adoption, with $2.45M vs $8.06M and 13% needed for the NRR target. Pro is shown at 20–33%, with 26% needed for the target and a ~21% break-even against the add-on. A Q3 gate at ≥13% is set. The 6% run-cost cover and the ~20% year-one payback thresholds for the add-on are not given.

Slides 8, 10 and 13 show cost per account by usage level and company gross margin: Pro with allowance 76.3%, Pro without allowance at 6,800 requests 74.1%, and the 35% price-fall upside 76.9%. The allowance holds the floor at $0.009. The usage thresholds at which the add-on or Pro break (e.g. ~4,100 or ~5,300 requests) are not given. The downside of a 2028 price rise is described, not quantified.

Slide 6 gives the win-rate benefit as a range ($0.64M to $0.32M) and rebuts the Sales claim. Slides 12 and 13 vary mobile churn prevented at 25–75% ($0.27–0.82M) and name a flip point. The flip is stated as '≥75%', but the slide 12 figures flip at about 51% (1.09 × share vs ≤$0.56M), which is internally inconsistent.

overclaim.quote: Launch Copilot in Q2 2027 inside a per-seat Pro plan: it is the only option that lifts NRR toward 105% and keeps gross margin above 75%

omissions: The headline '+3.0–5.0 NRR points' and 'only order that reaches 105% by H1 2028' are not netted against the document's own mobile-delay churn cost ($0.27–0.82M, about 0.5–1.4 pts). At 20% migration, Pro alone is 3.0 pts, below the 4-pt target. The 26% needed to reach the target exceeds the 20% low case.

Slide 13 says mobile-first loses less ARR only at ≥75% churn prevented, but slide 12's numbers (≤$0.56M vs 1.09 × share) cross at about 51%, and lower if AI explains less of the win-rate drop. The decision-critical flip point is misstated, and the 'close call' framing hides that the central case is roughly a tie.

No test of a hard-capped free-in-Core variant (cap ~1,070 requests per account, which is below the beta median), nor of an add-on with a lower entry price plus usage charges. Both alternatives are rejected only in their uncapped or flat forms.

No evidence on whether a 500-requests-per-seat pooled allowance (3,100 for an average account) leaves the heavy users who drive demand (paywall buyers average 6,800) willing to pay. Pack uptake and price for $200 per 10,000 are unvalidated, yet the margin guardrail depends on them.
unsupported_assumptions: "Share of accounts that move to Pro within 12 months: base 33%, as in the 2023 tier launch (20–33%)" — a different tier, with no AI and a different price step, is used as the base case. The 20% low case has no stated basis. The document treats the volunteer 14% as a ceiling but not this precedent.
"Adjust for larger beta accounts 14% → 10.7%" — scaling purchase propensity by 6.2 ÷ 8.1 seats is the document's own assumption, with no evidence that adoption scales with seat count.

"Share of mobile churn the rewrite prevents: 50% (25–75%)" — the pack gives no estimate. The recommendation to launch first and the claim that Copilot first 'reaches 105% about two quarters sooner' rest on this, and on 'late 2028 at best, likely to slip' for mobile-first, which has no support.

"Size of accounts that move to Pro: Average, 6.2 seats" and "Pro AI cost at the full allowance (3,100 requests per average account)" — assumes migrators are average size and that usage is capped at the allowance, while the evidence says adopters are larger and heavier. Pro margins of 76.3–76.5% depend on both.
"Packs of 10,000 requests for $200 a month … 55% margin on packs" — a price chosen without willingness-to-pay evidence.
